# Tools and alternatives

Every tool Deskfern names is scored here with the shared method (six criteria, an evidence line for each, closeness to the paid reference, a plain recommendation by user type). Scores are judgements from sources and our own adapter work on the date shown, not benchmarks. Anything not run against the real vendor says so. No price figures are quoted because none were read from a vendor page today.

<!-- SCORES:START (generated by tools/score_tools.py, do not edit by hand) -->

Scores dated 2026-11-23. Judgements from sources and our own adapter work on the date shown, not benchmarks. A tool marked not run was scored from its description only, and a source marked not fetched was not read.

### Help desk (where customers write and where drafts are sent from)

| Tool | Kind | Fit (35) | Setup effort (15) | Reliability and upkeep (15) | Cost (15) | Data control (10) | Integration depth (10) | Total | Closeness |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Intercom | paid | 75 | 60 | 80 | 50 | 50 | 55 | **65.2** | reference |
| Chatwoot | open_source | 78 | 55 | 70 | 85 | 90 | 75 | **75.3** | 104 percent of Intercom |
| Zendesk | paid | 72 | 60 | 85 | 45 | 50 | 50 | **63.7** | 96 percent of Intercom |
| Freshdesk | paid | 70 | 65 | 78 | 55 | 50 | 50 | **64.2** | 93 percent of Intercom |

What Deskfern has for each: Intercom: Adapter written from memory, tested against a stand in (not run against Intercom); Chatwoot: Adapter tested against a stand in, webhook signature rule read from the vendor (not run against Chatwoot); Zendesk: Adapter written from memory, tested against a stand in (not run against Zendesk); Freshdesk: Adapter written from memory, tested against a stand in (not run against Freshdesk).

**Evidence, Intercom**

- Fit (75): Strong AI help desk with its own answer product, so Deskfern overlaps with it. Our adapter reads conversations and posts replies and notes.
- Setup effort (60): Needs an access token from the developer hub. Not run here, judged from the steps.
- Reliability and upkeep (80): Mature hosted service with wide use.
- Cost (50): Per seat and per resolution pricing in general. Not read today, no figures quoted.
- Data control (50): Data sits with the vendor, in the vendor's regions.
- Integration depth (55): Adapter covers list and reply only, written from memory and not run.
- Sources: https://developers.intercom.com/docs (checked not fetched (script rendered))

**Evidence, Chatwoot**

- Fit (78): Covers shared inbox, email and chat channels, which is what a small client needs. No built in answer engine, which Deskfern supplies.
- Setup effort (55): Self hosting needs Docker, a database and an email setup. A hosted plan exists too.
- Reliability and upkeep (70): Active project, but you own the upgrades when self hosted.
- Cost (85): Free to self host, you pay for the server and your time.
- Data control (90): Self hosting keeps every conversation on your own server.
- Integration depth (75): Webhook check follows the vendor's help article. The send path is UNVERIFIED because the developer docs page could not be read.
- Sources: https://www.chatwoot.com/hc/user-guide/articles/1677693021-how-to-use-webhooks (checked 2026-11-23 (signature headers and signed string read))

**Evidence, Zendesk**

- Fit (72): Full ticketing with SLAs and reporting. Deskfern adds cited drafts on top.
- Setup effort (60): Needs a subdomain, an agent email and an API token. Not run.
- Reliability and upkeep (85): Long established service.
- Cost (45): Per agent pricing in general. Not read today.
- Data control (50): Vendor hosted. This is a judgement, not a measurement.
- Integration depth (50): Reads open tickets and adds a comment. Written from memory, not run.
- Sources: https://developer.zendesk.com/api-reference/ (checked not fetched)

**Evidence, Freshdesk**

- Fit (70): Ticketing with automation and a friendly price ladder in general. Fits small teams.
- Setup effort (65): API key and domain are enough to start. Not run.
- Reliability and upkeep (78): Established service. This is a judgement, not a measurement.
- Cost (55): Has a free tier in general, not confirmed today.
- Data control (50): Vendor hosted. This is a judgement, not a measurement.
- Integration depth (50): Reads tickets and posts replies. Private notes are not built. Written from memory, not run.
- Sources: https://developers.freshdesk.com/api/ (checked not fetched)

**Recommendation by user type**

- **Beginner:** Use the help desk the client already has. If they have none, Chatwoot is a good first choice because Deskfern's webhook check for it was written from the vendor's own help article.
- **Implementer running it for clients:** Chatwoot is the best tested path here (signature check and send call against a stand in). Intercom, Zendesk and Freshdesk adapters are written from memory of public docs and need a test against the client's own account first.
- **Cost sensitive owner:** Chatwoot is open source and can be hosted for the cost of a small server. The paid desks have their own price pages, read them yourself before choosing.
- **When open source is the right call:** Open source is the right call when the client wants conversations on their own server, or a team is small and can run Docker. It is the wrong call when support staff already live in Intercom, Zendesk or Freshdesk.

### Search index for the knowledge base

| Tool | Kind | Fit (35) | Setup effort (15) | Reliability and upkeep (15) | Cost (15) | Data control (10) | Integration depth (10) | Total | Closeness |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Hosted vector database (for example Pinecone) | paid | 85 | 55 | 85 | 40 | 40 | 0 | **60.8** | reference |
| SQLite full text (FTS5) | open_source | 60 | 95 | 90 | 100 | 100 | 100 | **83.8** | 71 percent of Hosted vector database (for example Pinecone) |
| Postgres full text | open_source | 60 | 80 | 90 | 100 | 100 | 90 | **80.5** | 71 percent of Hosted vector database (for example Pinecone) |
| pgvector (Postgres extension) | open_source | 80 | 50 | 75 | 95 | 100 | 0 | **71.0** | 94 percent of Hosted vector database (for example Pinecone) |

What Deskfern has for each: Hosted vector database (for example Pinecone): Not built. Deskfern uses a hashed word vector stand in (not run); SQLite full text (FTS5): Built and tested (run in the tests and the demo); Postgres full text: Built, SQL path exercised in a throwaway Postgres 17 (run in a local test); pgvector (Postgres extension): Not built. Not installed in the local Postgres used here (not run).

**Evidence, Hosted vector database (for example Pinecone)**

- Fit (85): Meaning based search finds pages that share no words with the question, which is the weakness measured in this repo.
- Setup effort (55): Needs an account, an index and a way to make embeddings.
- Reliability and upkeep (85): Managed service. This is a judgement, not a measurement.
- Cost (40): Usage priced. Not read today.
- Data control (40): Documents and vectors leave your server.
- Integration depth (0): No adapter exists in Deskfern.
- Sources: https://docs.pinecone.io/ (checked not fetched)

**Evidence, SQLite full text (FTS5)**

- Fit (60): Word matching with ranking. Misses questions that use other words than the page, as the held out set shows.
- Setup effort (95): Ships inside Python, nothing to install.
- Reliability and upkeep (90): Very stable, runs in one file.
- Cost (100): Free. This is a judgement, not a measurement.
- Data control (100): Data stays in your database file.
- Integration depth (100): Used directly, with a rebuild step.
- Sources: https://www.sqlite.org/fts5.html (checked 2026-11-23 (BM25 and MATCH used as documented))

**Evidence, Postgres full text**

- Fit (60): Same word matching idea as SQLite, with stemming rules of its own.
- Setup effort (80): Already there when the client runs Postgres.
- Reliability and upkeep (90): Stable and widely run. This is a judgement, not a measurement.
- Cost (100): Free. This is a judgement, not a measurement.
- Data control (100): Stays in your database. This is a judgement, not a measurement.
- Integration depth (90): Deskfern stores stems and queries them with to_tsvector.
- Sources: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/textsearch.html (checked 2026-11-23)

**Evidence, pgvector (Postgres extension)**

- Fit (80): Would allow meaning based search inside Postgres if embeddings are produced elsewhere.
- Setup effort (50): Needs the extension on the host. Not present in the local Postgres 17 used for tests, and host support is UNVERIFIED.
- Reliability and upkeep (75): Well known extension. This is a judgement, not a measurement.
- Cost (95): Free, plus embedding costs.
- Data control (100): Stays in your database. This is a judgement, not a measurement.
- Integration depth (0): No adapter exists in Deskfern.
- Sources: https://github.com/pgvector/pgvector (checked not fetched)

**Recommendation by user type**

- **Beginner:** Keep the built in SQLite search for a demo and for a small help centre. You do not need to set up anything else.
- **Implementer running it for clients:** Use SQLite full text for a single client on one server, Postgres full text when the client runs on Postgres. Add real embeddings only after you measure that keyword search misses too many questions (the held out numbers in this repo show it does for wording that differs from the pages).
- **Cost sensitive owner:** Both full text options cost nothing extra. A hosted vector database adds a monthly bill and a second place your data lives.
- **When open source is the right call:** Open source search is the right call for a help centre of a few thousand pages. A hosted vector database is worth it when meaning based search over a large, changing set matters more than cost.

### Refunds (the only money movement)

| Tool | Kind | Fit (35) | Setup effort (15) | Reliability and upkeep (15) | Cost (15) | Data control (10) | Integration depth (10) | Total | Closeness |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Stripe refunds | paid | 85 | 70 | 90 | 60 | 60 | 80 | **76.8** | reference |

What Deskfern has for each: Stripe refunds: Adapter tested against a stand in (not run against Stripe).

**Evidence, Stripe refunds**

- Fit (85): Create refund call matches what Deskfern needs: a charge, an amount, a reason and metadata.
- Setup effort (70): Needs a secret or restricted key. Test mode makes a safe first run.
- Reliability and upkeep (90): Widely used and well documented.
- Cost (60): Priced as part of the processor. Not read today.
- Data control (60): Payment data stays with Stripe, Deskfern stores only a charge id.
- Integration depth (80): Adapter sends an idempotency key so a retry cannot pay twice. Not run live.
- Sources: https://docs.stripe.com/api/refunds/create (checked 2026-11-23 (endpoint, parameters and idempotency read))

**Recommendation by user type**

- **Beginner:** If the client takes cards with Stripe, use it. Keep MODE=draft until a person has approved a test refund in Stripe's test mode.
- **Implementer running it for clients:** Stripe is the only refund adapter. It is tested only against a stand in. Use a restricted key that can write refunds only, and keep the approval step on.
- **Cost sensitive owner:** Refunds themselves are a normal part of the card processor's pricing. Check the current price page yourself.
- **When open source is the right call:** There is no open source way to refund a card payment. For other processors write an adapter from the recipe prompt.

### Where the knowledge lives

| Tool | Kind | Fit (35) | Setup effort (15) | Reliability and upkeep (15) | Cost (15) | Data control (10) | Integration depth (10) | Total | Closeness |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Google Drive | paid | 70 | 50 | 85 | 80 | 45 | 50 | **66.2** | reference |
| Notion | paid | 70 | 55 | 80 | 75 | 45 | 45 | **65.0** | 100 percent of Google Drive |
| Local folder (Markdown, text, PDF) | open_source | 75 | 95 | 90 | 100 | 100 | 100 | **89.0** | 107 percent of Google Drive |

What Deskfern has for each: Google Drive: Read only adapter tested against a stand in (not run against Google); Notion: Read only adapter tested against a stand in (not run against Notion); Local folder (Markdown, text, PDF): Built and tested (run in the tests and the demo).

**Evidence, Google Drive**

- Fit (70): Many teams keep policies as Google Docs. Deskfern exports a document as plain text.
- Setup effort (50): Needs an OAuth token with read only scope. The sign in steps are not covered by the adapter.
- Reliability and upkeep (85): Reliable. This is a judgement, not a measurement.
- Cost (80): Usually already paid for.
- Data control (45): Documents stay with Google, Deskfern stores a copy of the text.
- Integration depth (50): Lists documents and exports text. Written from memory, not run.
- Sources: https://developers.google.com/drive/api (checked not fetched)

**Evidence, Notion**

- Fit (70): Common home for help pages. Blocks are read as paragraphs, tables and embeds are not.
- Setup effort (55): Needs an internal integration token and pages shared with it.
- Reliability and upkeep (80): Reliable, with rate limits.
- Cost (75): Usually already paid for.
- Data control (45): Pages stay with Notion, Deskfern stores a copy.
- Integration depth (45): Searches pages and reads block text. Written from memory, not run.
- Sources: https://developers.notion.com/ (checked not fetched)

**Evidence, Local folder (Markdown, text, PDF)**

- Fit (75): Covers the common case: exported help pages and policy PDFs. PDFs with scanned images are not read.
- Setup effort (95): Point it at a folder. This is a judgement, not a measurement.
- Reliability and upkeep (90): Plain files, easy to back up and review.
- Cost (100): Free. This is a judgement, not a measurement.
- Data control (100): Everything stays on your server.
- Integration depth (100): Built into Deskfern, skips links that point outside the folder and files over 10 MB.
- Sources: https://pypi.org/project/pypdf/ (checked 2026-11-23 (library used for PDFs))

**Recommendation by user type**

- **Beginner:** Start with a folder of Markdown or PDF files. It needs no account and is the best tested source.
- **Implementer running it for clients:** Use the folder source for anything you can export. Drive and Notion adapters are read only and written from memory, test each against the client's own workspace first.
- **Cost sensitive owner:** A folder costs nothing. Drive and Notion are usually already paid for by the client.
- **When open source is the right call:** A plain folder (or a Git repo of Markdown) is the right call when the client wants control and a clean history. Use Drive or Notion when staff already write the help pages there.

### Who writes the answer sentences

| Tool | Kind | Fit (35) | Setup effort (15) | Reliability and upkeep (15) | Cost (15) | Data control (10) | Integration depth (10) | Total | Closeness |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Language model (Anthropic API) | paid | 90 | 60 | 85 | 50 | 50 | 40 | **69.8** | reference |
| Offline rules writer (built in) | open_source | 40 | 100 | 95 | 100 | 100 | 100 | **78.2** | 44 percent of Language model (Anthropic API) |

What Deskfern has for each: Language model (Anthropic API): Plug in written against the base wrapper, never run (not run); Offline rules writer (built in): Built and tested (run in the tests and the demo).

**Evidence, Language model (Anthropic API)**

- Fit (90): Can phrase one answer from several pages and handle other wording and languages, which the offline writer cannot.
- Setup effort (60): Needs an API key. This is a judgement, not a measurement.
- Reliability and upkeep (85): Hosted service with limits.
- Cost (50): Priced per token. Not read today.
- Data control (50): Ticket text leaves the server, wrapped as untrusted data.
- Integration depth (40): The writer interface exists and the groundedness check judges its output. Never run live.
- Sources: https://docs.anthropic.com/ (checked not fetched)

**Evidence, Offline rules writer (built in)**

- Fit (40): Copies the best source sentences. First run on the held out set: see docs/ANSWER-EVAL.md, it is weak on different wording.
- Setup effort (100): Nothing to set up. This is a judgement, not a measurement.
- Reliability and upkeep (95): Deterministic, same input same output.
- Cost (100): Free. This is a judgement, not a measurement.
- Data control (100): Nothing leaves the server.
- Integration depth (100): Built in. This is a judgement, not a measurement.
- Sources: data/eval/heldout_first_run.json (checked 2026-11-23 (our own first run numbers))

**Recommendation by user type**

- **Beginner:** Use the offline rules writer to try the product. It copies sentences from your pages, which is dull but never invents anything.
- **Implementer running it for clients:** Measure before you switch: run the held out questions and the test cases with the model writer in a test account, and keep the groundedness check on whatever writes the words.
- **Cost sensitive owner:** The offline writer costs nothing. A model writer costs per use. Read the price page yourself.
- **When open source is the right call:** There is no open source model scored here. Self hosted models are possible but were not tried.

### Where Deskfern runs

| Tool | Kind | Fit (35) | Setup effort (15) | Reliability and upkeep (15) | Cost (15) | Data control (10) | Integration depth (10) | Total | Closeness |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Railway | paid | 80 | 85 | 80 | 65 | 55 | 70 | **75.0** | reference |
| Vercel | paid | 80 | 90 | 85 | 65 | 55 | 75 | **77.0** | 100 percent of Railway |
| Hetzner VPS with Docker Compose | paid | 85 | 50 | 80 | 90 | 85 | 75 | **78.8** | 106 percent of Railway |

What Deskfern has for each: Railway: Config written, not deployed (not run); Vercel: Web app config written, not deployed (not run); Hetzner VPS with Docker Compose: Compose, Caddy and cloud init written, not deployed (not run).

**Evidence, Railway**

- Fit (80): Runs the API and the worker from one repo with a Postgres add on.
- Setup effort (85): Connect the repo and set variables.
- Reliability and upkeep (80): Managed platform. This is a judgement, not a measurement.
- Cost (65): Usage priced. Not read today.
- Data control (55): Vendor hosted. This is a judgement, not a measurement.
- Integration depth (70): Dockerfiles and a railway.json are in the repo. Not deployed.
- Sources: https://docs.railway.com/ (checked not fetched)

**Evidence, Vercel**

- Fit (80): Hosts the Next.js web app only. The API must run elsewhere.
- Setup effort (90): Import the repo and set the root directory to apps/web.
- Reliability and upkeep (85): Managed platform. This is a judgement, not a measurement.
- Cost (65): Free and paid tiers. Not read today.
- Data control (55): Vendor hosted. This is a judgement, not a measurement.
- Integration depth (75): Needs API_BASE_URL and SESSION_SECRET. Not deployed.
- Sources: https://vercel.com/docs/monorepos (checked 2026-11-23 (root directory setting for a monorepo))

**Evidence, Hetzner VPS with Docker Compose**

- Fit (85): Runs everything in one place, including Postgres and automatic HTTPS through Caddy.
- Setup effort (50): You manage the server, firewall and updates.
- Reliability and upkeep (80): As reliable as you keep it.
- Cost (90): Among the cheapest options in general. Not read today.
- Data control (85): You choose the region and hold the data.
- Integration depth (75): Compose file, Caddyfile, backup script and cloud init are in the repo. Not run.
- Sources: https://docs.hetzner.com/ (checked not fetched)

**Recommendation by user type**

- **Beginner:** Vercel for the web part and Railway for the API and worker is the least work.
- **Implementer running it for clients:** Hetzner with Docker Compose when you run several clients and want one bill and full control. Keep the web on Vercel if you like preview deploys.
- **Cost sensitive owner:** A small Hetzner server is the cheapest for the API. Check current prices yourself.
- **When open source is the right call:** Self hosting is the right call when data must stay in one place you control. It costs your time for updates and backups.

### Named but not scored

- Gmail and Outlook mailboxes: Work through the generic IMAP adapter only if the account allows it. Not tested.
- Other help desks and processors: No adapter. Use the recipe prompts to have Claude Code or Codex write one.
